name: CoQ10 mesotherapy

lead: Coenzyme Q10 is a naturally occurring antioxidant, and clinics include it in mesotherapy 'cocktails' alongside ingredients such as vitamins and hyaluronic acid. The aim is a more hydrated, radiant, refreshed-looking face.

Mesotherapy itself is injection of small amounts of substances just under the skin. Wikipedia reports that cosmetic uses have not been tested in standard clinical trials, and that a 10-patient facial study found no clinically relevant rejuvenation.

paras: Practitioners place small superficial injections across the face, neck or hands, often in a series of sessions, with CoQ10 as one component of a blend. Specific products and protocols vary by clinic.

Wikipedia describes infections (abscesses and a mycobacterial infection in one Australian salon case) and inflammation with some injected substances, and notes regulation varies, with some South American countries banning it for certain uses.

chain: Antioxidant blend placed in the superficial skin
angle.text: Clinics include CoQ10 in mesotherapy blends to give skin a fresher, more radiant look, as part of a series of superficial injection sessions.

lead: CoQ10 mesotherapy refers to blends containing coenzyme Q10 that are delivered by mesotherapy, the practice of injecting small amounts of drugs, enzymes, vitamins, plant extracts or hyaluronic acid just beneath the skin [1]. In aesthetic clinics it is offered with the goal of hydrating the skin and refreshing its look [1].

Mesotherapy was developed by Michel Pistor, and the French press coined the term in 1958; the French Academy of Medicine recognised it as a specialty in 1987 [1]. Wikipedia states cosmetic uses have not been tested in standard clinical trials and cites a 10-patient facial study that found no clinically relevant skin-rejuvenation benefit [1]. No published trial has tested CoQ10 mesotherapy specifically.

paras: Mesotherapy blends are customised by practitioners and may include vitamins, hyaluronic acid and plant extracts alongside other agents [1]. CoQ10 is marketed as one antioxidant ingredient among them.

Reports include skin abscesses and a mycobacterial infection after treatment in one Australian salon, and extreme inflammation attributed by a dermatologist to phosphatidylcholine [1]. In the US the FDA does not control what practitioners inject, as state medical boards oversee practice; several South American countries have banned mesotherapy for some uses [1]. A 2011 French ban on mesotherapy for fat removal was lifted after an investigation attributed problems to hygiene [1].
No studies found for CoQ10 mesotherapy specifically. For mesotherapy generally, a 10-patient facial study found no clinically relevant rejuvenation benefit, according to Wikipedia [1].

timeline.event: The term mesotherapy is coined by the French press [1].
The French Academy of Medicine recognises mesotherapy [1].
